q: On a night passage along the Turkish coast you come on deck and find the watch like this. What is missing under Rule 5?
a: A look-out by sight and hearing, all round
o: Nothing — radar and AIS are the look-out
A radar guard zone set to 6 miles
An AIS alarm set to a 2-mile CPA
why: Rule 5: a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means — electronics add to it, never replace it.

q: A charter yacht on port tack is closing with nobody in her cockpit. How does Rule 2 answer your crew?
a: No rule excuses you from good seamanship
o: Right — the stand-on yacht is never to blame
Right — until she sounds five short blasts
Right — if you hold course and speed exactly
why: Rule 2(a): nothing in the Rules excuses the neglect of any precaution required by the ordinary practice of seamen.

fig.title: Your crew's view
lines: “She's on port tack, we're on starboard”
“If she hits us, it's all her fault”

q: You are the stand-on vessel, but holding your course and speed will put you on the rock in two minutes. What do the rules allow?
a: Turn away from the rock now, clearly
o: Hold on — the stand-on must keep her course
Hold on until she has passed, then turn
Turn only after sounding five short blasts
why: Rule 2(b): a departure from the Rules is required to avoid immediate danger — here a danger of navigation.

fig.title: Standing on, under sail
lines: Motor yacht crossing, slow to give way

q: Beating into a short sea off Cavtat with the mainsail up, you put the engine in gear to help. Your crew hoists this shape forward. What does it say?
a: You are now a power-driven vessel
o: You are still a sailing vessel
You are restricted in your ability to manoeuvre
You are a sailing vessel with right of way
why: Rule 3: a sailing vessel using her engine is power-driven; Rule 25(e): she shows a cone, point down, forward.

fig.note: Day · hoisted forward

q: Close-hauled along the Dalmatian coast, you converge with this motor boat trolling two lines astern for tuna. She shows no shape. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — trolling lines don't make her fishing
o: You do — any boat fishing has right of way
You do — she is on your starboard bow
Both alter to starboard as if head-on
why: Rule 3(d): trolling lines do not restrict manoeuvrability, so she is simply power-driven; Rule 18: power keeps clear of sail.

fig.note: Two trolling lines astern · bearing steady

q: Mid-Channel in thick fog you stop the engine and drift to listen for ships. Which fog signal do you sound?
a: Two prolonged blasts every two minutes or less
o: One prolonged blast every two minutes or less
One prolonged and two short every two minutes
Rapid ringing of the bell every minute
why: With no sail set you are power-driven; underway with no way on, Rule 35(b): two prolonged blasts, at most 2 minutes apart.

fig.title: Fog, waiting to listen
lines: 13 m yacht, sails down, engine stopped
Drifting — not at anchor, no way on

q: On passage through a heavy rainstorm, your crew says the radar screen is clear, so you can keep 7 kn. What does Rule 6 say?
a: Small craft can hide in clutter — slow down
o: The radar is the look-out — keep 7 kn
Safe speed is anything under hull speed
Slow down only once a target appears
why: Rule 6(b): small vessels may not be detected at an adequate range in sea and rain clutter — keep a speed you can stop in.

fig.title: Heavy rain, radar on
lines: Moderate sea, clutter out to 1.5 M

q: Motoring on a steady course at night, you plot this ship on radar every six minutes. What do you conclude?
a: Risk of collision — the bearing is not changing
o: No risk — the bearing has moved by 1°
No risk yet — check again at 1 mile
Risk only once she is inside 2 miles
why: Rule 7(d)(i): risk is deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change.

q: Under engine by day, you watch this tug crossing ahead of you with a long tow. Is there a risk of collision?
a: It may exist — a tow brings risk despite the change
o: No — the tug's bearing is clearly changing
No — the bearing draws right, she'll pass ahead
No — a tug with a tow always keeps clear
why: Rule 7(d)(ii): risk may exist despite an appreciable bearing change, especially with a large vessel, a tow, or at close range.

fig.title: Tug and tow ahead
lines: Range to the tug 1.2 M, closing

q: You are motoring at 6 kn with plenty of sea room. This ship is crossing from your starboard side. What do you do?
a: One bold turn to starboard, early, to pass astern
o: Slow down by 2 knots and hold your course
Three 10° turns to starboard, one by one
A small turn to port to pass ahead of her
why: Rules 15, 16, 8: keep clear and don't cross ahead; one large early turn is seen, small steps or a speed change are not.

fig.note: Bearing steady · 3 M · she makes 18 kn

q: You want to cross this narrow buoyed channel to reach the marina on the far side. The ferry is 1 M away, coming down the channel. What do you do?
a: Wait, and cross astern of her once she is clear
o: Cross now — you are on her starboard bow
Cross now at full speed, at right angles
Cross now, sounding one short blast
why: Rule 9(d): do not cross a narrow channel if it impedes a vessel that can safely navigate only within it.

fig.note: Buoyed channel · she can only use the channel

q: You are motoring up a narrow channel, keeping to its starboard side. A ship astern sounds two prolonged blasts and two short. What does she mean, and what do you do?
a: She'll pass on your port side — agree, give room
o: She'll pass on your starboard side — agree, give room
She is turning to starboard — hold your course
She doubts your intentions — stop at once
why: Rule 34(c): two prolonged + two short = I intend to overtake on your port side; agree with — · — · and make room.

q: Motoring up this river channel, you approach a bend where high wooded banks hide anything coming the other way. Which sound signal do you make?
a: One prolonged blast
o: Two prolonged blasts
Five short and rapid blasts
One short blast
why: Rule 34(e): one prolonged blast nearing a bend where other vessels may be hidden; a vessel beyond answers with one prolonged.

fig.note: River · the bend is hidden by the banks

q: Motoring from the coast, you want to join the eastbound lane of this scheme from its side, not at its end. How do you enter it?
a: At as small an angle to the traffic flow as you can
o: At right angles to the flow, to be quick
Across the separation zone from the north
Only at the lane's end — never from the side
why: Rule 10(b)(iii): join a lane at its end, or from the side at as small an angle to the general direction of traffic as practicable.

fig.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

q: You must cross this scheme to the north in a 6-knot boat, with the stream setting east as the panel shows. Which heading do you steer across the lanes?
a: 000°T — the heading at right angles to the flow
o: 341°T — so the track crosses at right angles
019°T — the tide angle laid off the other way
090°T — along the lane to its far end
why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the traffic flow — the heading, not the track.

fig.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

q: Your crew says that to pass this headland you must go out and use the traffic lanes. What does Rule 10 say?
a: You may use the inshore traffic zone
o: You must use the lane for your direction
You may use it only if bound to a port in it
You may use it only between sunset and sunrise
why: Rule 10(d): vessels under 20 m, sailing vessels and vessels fishing may use an inshore traffic zone.

fig.title: Passing a headland with a TSS
lines: Inshore traffic zone along the coast
Your next port lies beyond the scheme

q: Under sail, you are crossing the lanes of a traffic separation scheme. This ship is following the lane. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you must not impede her in the lane
o: She does — power keeps clear of sail
She does — you are on her starboard side
Both alter course to starboard
why: Rule 10(j): a sailing vessel or one under 20 m shall not impede a power-driven vessel following a traffic lane.

fig.note: Eastbound lane of a TSS · bearing steady

q: Beating along the coast of Kefalonia, you and this yacht are on the same tack and converging. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you are the windward yacht
o: She does — she is on your port side
She does — she is the leeward yacht
You both tack away at once
why: Rule 12(a)(ii): on the same tack, the vessel to windward keeps out of the way of the vessel to leeward.

fig.note: Both on starboard tack · converging

q: Close-hauled on port tack at dusk, you cannot tell which tack this yacht to windward is on. What does Rule 12 tell you?
a: Keep clear of her — you can't be sure
o: Stand on — she is to windward of you
Stand on — a running yacht keeps clear
Hail her, and stand on until she answers
why: Rule 12(a)(iii): on port tack, if you can't tell the tack of a vessel to windward, you keep out of her way.

fig.title: Port tack, at dusk
lines: A yacht runs down towards you from upwind
Spinnaker set — you can't see her main

q: Ten minutes ago you came up from astern of this slower motor yacht. Now nearly abeam, the two of you are converging. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you are still the overtaking vessel
o: She does — you are on her starboard side
She does — overtaking ends once abeam
Both alter to starboard as if head-on
why: Rule 13(d): a later change of bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing one; keep clear until past and clear.

fig.note: You came up from astern of her · now converging

q: Motoring across the Strait of Otranto at 0100, you see these lights fine on your starboard bow. They hold their bearing. What do you do?
a: Alter boldly to starboard — she is head-on
o: Alter to port — open the gap to starboard
Hold on — she is crossing, you stand on
Slow down and let her pass ahead of you
why: Rule 14: masthead lights nearly in line and both sidelights — head-on; each alters to starboard and passes port to port.

fig.note: Night · fine on your starboard bow, steady

q: On a night passage under engine from Split to Vis, these lights open on your port bow and keep the same compass bearing for ten minutes. What do you do?
a: Hold your course and speed, and watch her
o: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Turn to starboard to pass astern of her
Slow down and let her cross ahead
why: She shows green: you are on her starboard side, so she gives way (Rule 15); you stand on and watch her (Rule 17).

fig.note: Night · on your port bow, bearing steady

q: Under power south of Mykonos after midnight, you pick up these lights to starboard, closing on a steady bearing. What is she, and who keeps clear?
a: A vessel under sail — you keep clear
o: A vessel motor-sailing — she keeps clear
A vessel not under command — you keep clear
A power vessel under 12 m — she keeps clear
why: Rule 25(c): all-round red over green at the masthead = sailing; Rule 18: you, under power, keep out of her way.

fig.note: Night · on your starboard bow, bearing steady

q: You are the stand-on vessel under power. She has not altered, and your five short blasts got no answer. You decide to act. What do you do?
a: Turn to starboard or slow down — never to port
o: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Hold course and speed — you must stand on
Speed up to cross ahead of her quickly
why: Rule 17(a)(ii) lets you act; 17(c): a power vessel shall not, if avoidable, alter to port for a vessel on her own port side.

fig.note: Five short sounded · no response · closing

q: You hold your course and speed as this ship closes. At what point does Rule 17 say you MUST act yourself?
a: When she alone can no longer avoid collision
o: As soon as risk of collision first exists
As soon as you have sounded five short
Never — the stand-on vessel holds on
why: Rule 17(a)(ii): you may act once she clearly isn't; 17(b): you must, when collision can't be avoided by her action alone.

fig.title: Stand-on, under power
lines: Ship crossing from your port side
She has made no move to give way

q: In open water off Kavala, these three vessels are converging. Which of them must keep out of the way of both the others?
a: A — you, under sail
o: B — the trawler, trawling
C — the dredger, working
None — all turn to starboard
why: Rule 18: sail keeps clear of fishing and of RAM; fishing keeps clear of RAM. The working dredger stands on.

q: In fog, you have this radar target fine on your port bow, closing. You decide to alter course. Which way?
a: To starboard, away from her side
o: To port — she will then pass to starboard
Either way — fog suspends the steering rules
No turn — you are the stand-on vessel
why: Rule 19(d)(i): for a vessel detected forward of the beam, avoid an alteration to port (unless she is being overtaken).

fig.note: Fog · radar only · CPA under 2 cables

q: Motoring in fog, you hear this signal and can see nothing on the radar. What does Rule 19 require you to do?
a: Slow to bare steerage way; stop if need be
o: Turn hard to port, away from the sound
Hold speed and sound five short blasts
Speed up to clear the area quickly
why: Rule 19(e): on hearing a fog signal forward of the beam, cut to the least speed to keep your course; take all way off if necessary.

fig.title: Fog, motoring at 6 kn
lines: Heard forward of your starboard beam

q: Your crew says: “We're under sail, so she must keep clear of us.” What do you do?
a: Act early yourself — in fog nobody stands on
o: Stand on — power keeps clear of sail
Stand on — you are on her starboard side
Turn to port to pass ahead of her
why: Rule 19 governs vessels not in sight of one another: no stand-on vessel; each takes avoiding action in ample time.

fig.title: Fog, under sail
lines: Radar: ship 3 M on your port bow

q: Fitting out for a night passage, you look at the box of the new sidelights. Do they meet the rules for your yacht?
a: No — 12 to 50 m needs sidelights seen at 2 M
o: Yes — 1 M is enough for a yacht under 20 m
Yes — the rules set no range for sidelights
No — over 12 m they must be seen at 3 M
why: Rule 22: sidelights are seen at 1 M under 12 m, 2 M from 12 to 50 m, and 3 M at 50 m or more.

fig.title: Your yacht
lines: New LED sidelights to be fitted

q: Under engine, you are catching up this yacht from right astern and draw out onto her starboard side. When will her green sidelight come into view?
a: When you are 22.5° abaft her beam
o: When you are exactly abeam of her
When you are 45° abaft her beam
When you are ahead of her beam
why: Rule 21: a sidelight shows from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam; the sternlight covers the 135° astern.

fig.note: Night · a yacht ahead, you are gaining

q: On a night passage you furl the genoa and start the engine, mainsail still up. Which switches do you turn on?
a: Steaming light, and the bow and stern lights
o: Tricolour and the steaming light together
Tricolour only — the main is still up
Steaming light and the anchor light
why: Under engine you are power-driven (Rule 23): masthead light, sidelights and sternlight. The tricolour is for sail alone.

q: Under sail at night, you see these lights dead ahead, low down and closing fast. What is she?
a: A motor boat under 12 m, head-on
o: A sailing yacht under 20 m, head-on
A vessel at anchor with her deck lit
A ship over 50 m, crossing ahead
why: Rule 23(d): a power vessel under 12 m may show one all-round white with sidelights instead of masthead light and sternlight.

fig.note: Night · dead ahead, closing fast

q: On a night sail from Zakynthos to Kalamata, these lights sit on your starboard bow and the hand-bearing compass shows no change. Who gives way?
a: You — she is trawling
o: She does — power gives way to sail
She does — she is a pilot boat at work
You — she is not under command
why: Rule 26(b): all-round green over white = trawling; Rule 18(b): a sailing vessel keeps out of the way of a vessel fishing.

fig.note: Night · on your starboard bow, bearing steady

q: Under sail at night, you want to pass this vessel about a mile ahead. Which side do you pass her?
a: To the left, away from the lone white light
o: To the right, on the lone white light's side
Between the red-white pair and the lone white
Either side — she is not making way
why: Rule 26(c)(ii): an all-round white beside the red over white shows gear out over 150 m that way — pass on the other side.

fig.note: Night · about 1 M ahead, no sidelights

q: At night off the Peloponnese you see these lights on your starboard bow. What do they tell you?
a: Not under command, and making way
o: Not under command, and stopped
Aground — keep well clear of her
Constrained by her draught
why: Rule 27(a): two all-round reds = not under command; she adds sidelights and a sternlight only when making way.

fig.note: Night · on your starboard bow

q: Motoring towards Brindisi in the dark, you have these lights on your port bow, the compass bearing unchanged. Who has to keep clear?
a: You — she is restricted in ability to manoeuvre
o: She does — you are on her starboard side
You — she is only a pilot vessel on duty
She does — she is a tug with a short tow
why: Rule 27(b): red-white-red all-round = restricted in ability to manoeuvre; with masthead light and sidelight she is making way.

fig.note: Night · on your port bow, bearing steady

q: Motoring out along the main channel of a big port at night, you see these lights dead ahead in the channel. What do you do?
a: Keep well to starboard and don't impede her
o: Alter to port — she will pass to starboard
Hold your course in mid-channel
Stop in mid-channel until she has passed
why: Rule 28: three all-round reds = constrained by her draught; Rules 9 and 18(d): keep to starboard and avoid impeding her.

fig.note: Night · dead ahead in the channel

q: Approaching a busy port at night, you see these lights off the entrance. What is she?
a: A pilot vessel on duty, under way
o: A vessel fishing, other than trawling
A pilot vessel on duty, at anchor
A vessel not under command
why: Rule 29: all-round white over red at the masthead = pilot on duty; with sidelights she is under way.

fig.note: Night · off the harbour entrance

q: Motoring at night, you are slowly catching up these lights. No other lights are in sight. What should worry you?
a: She is towing — her tow lies between you and her
o: She is at anchor — pass her on either side
She is towing — her tow is ahead of her
She is pushing ahead — nothing is astern of her
why: Rule 24: the yellow towing light above the sternlight is shown by the towing vessel — her tow follows astern of her.

fig.note: Night · ahead, on your course, you are gaining

q: Under engine at night, you see these lights dead ahead. What do they tell you?
a: A tug head-on with a tow over 200 m long
o: A tug head-on with a tow under 200 m long
Three vessels in line, one behind another
A vessel restricted in her manoeuvring
why: Rule 24(a): three masthead lights in a vertical line = towing, the tow longer than 200 m from her stern to its end.

fig.note: Night · dead ahead, bearing steady

q: You anchor your 11 m yacht for lunch in a bay off Hvar, among other yachts. The crew asks if you really need this shape. What do the rules say?
a: Yes — only boats under 7 m, clear of traffic, are exempt
o: No — yachts under 12 m are exempt by day
No — the shape is needed only in fog
No — it is needed only in a channel
why: Rule 30(a),(e): a ball forward at anchor; only vessels under 7 m clear of channels, anchorages and traffic are exempt.

fig.note: Hoisted forward, at anchor

q: Under sail off Rovinj, you approach this vessel working beside a navigation buoy. What does her shape tell you?
a: She is restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
o: She is not under command after a breakdown
She is constrained by her draught
She is at anchor and working on deck
why: Rule 27(b): ball-diamond-ball = restricted in ability to manoeuvre, e.g. servicing a mark; Rule 18: keep out of her way.

fig.note: Day · working beside a buoy

q: By day you see this coaster with this shape on the edge of a sandbank. If she is still there tonight, what lights will she show?
a: Anchor lights plus two all-round reds
o: Three all-round reds, one above another
Two all-round reds and nothing else
Red, white and red, all-round
why: Rule 30(d): aground — three balls by day; at night her anchor lights and two all-round reds in a vertical line.

fig.note: Day · on the edge of a sandbank

q: Leaving Rhodes harbour, you watch a ferry back off the quay. As she swings, she sounds two short blasts. What does she mean?
a: I am altering my course to port
o: I am altering my course to starboard
I am operating astern propulsion
I intend to overtake you on your port side
why: Rule 34(a): one short — altering to starboard; two short — altering to port; three short — operating astern propulsion.

q: You are crossing this narrow channel under engine when the ship sounds five short, rapid blasts. What does she mean, and what do you do?
a: She doubts your intentions — get out of her way
o: She is turning to port — hold your course
She has stopped her engines — cross ahead
She is in distress — close her to help
why: Rule 34(d): five or more short rapid blasts = I doubt your action; make your intention plain and keep out of her way (Rule 9).

fig.title: Narrow channel, motoring
lines: You are crossing to the far side
A ship is coming down the channel
She sounds five short, rapid blasts

q: You are beating across the Channel in fog, under sail alone. Which fog signal do you sound?
a: One prolonged and two short every 2 minutes
o: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes
Two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes
One short, one prolonged, one short
why: Rule 35(c): a sailing vessel sounds one prolonged blast followed by two short, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.

q: Besides ringing your bell rapidly every minute, what may you also sound to warn the approaching vessel?
a: One short, one prolonged and one short blast
o: Three strokes on the bell before and after
One prolonged and two short blasts
Two prolonged blasts every two minutes
why: Rule 35(g): a vessel at anchor may also sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to warn of her position.

q: Hove-to in fog, you hear these signals, repeated. What is out there?
a: A tug and her manned tow — keep well clear
o: Two sailing yachts close together
A vessel aground and her attending tug
A fishing vessel and her outlying nets
why: Rule 35(c),(e): the tug sounds one prolonged + two short; the manned tow follows at once with one prolonged + three short.

fig.title: Fog, listening
lines: Then at once: one prolonged + three short

q: Crossing to Kos at dusk, you pass this motor boat a mile off. What is she telling you?
a: She is in distress and needs help
o: She is fishing — keep clear of her nets
She has divers down — keep clear, slow
She wants a pilot to come aboard
why: Annex IV: orange smoke, and a square flag with a ball above or below it, are both signals of distress.

fig.title: A mile off, at dusk
lines: A square flag with a ball below it

q: Motoring along the coast at midday, you run into this squall. Your crew asks whether the fog rules apply, lights and sound signals included. What do you tell them?
a: Yes — heavy rain is restricted visibility
o: No — only fog counts as restricted visibility
Lights yes, but sound signals only in fog
No — by day you never need navigation lights
why: Rule 3(l): heavy rain is restricted visibility; Rule 20(c) wants your lights on in it by day, Rule 35 the sound signals.

fig.title: Midday, heavy rain squall
lines: Motoring at 6 kn along the coast
Other boats about, out of sight

q: On a night beat along the Croatian coast, you take over the watch and find the boat set up like this. What does a proper look-out need here?
a: A regular look under the genoa to leeward
o: Nothing more — the radar covers the lee bow
A look round only when the AIS alarm sounds
Nothing more — boats to leeward keep clear
why: Rule 5: a look-out by sight in every direction — the sector hidden by the genoa has to be checked, and often.

fig.title: 0100, close-hauled, port tack
lines: Lee bow hidden from the helm

q: Approaching Split harbour at night under engine, you see the scene in the card. What does Rule 6 say about your speed?
a: Slow down — shore lights can hide boat lights
o: Keep 7 kn — the harbour is brightly lit
Speed up — get through the traffic quickly
Keep 7 kn — radar sees through the glare
why: Rule 6(a)(iv): background light from the shore is a factor of safe speed — the lights of other vessels get lost in it.

fig.title: 2300, approaching Split at 7 kn
lines: The city lit up behind the harbour
Their lights hard to pick out

q: Under sail, you are about to cross this channel. When must you act so as not to impede the ship?
a: Now, early — before any risk of collision exists
o: Once a steady bearing shows a risk of collision
Once she sounds five short blasts at you
Once she is within about two miles of you
why: Rule 8(f): a vessel bound not to impede acts early, leaving room for the other's safe passage — before any risk develops.

fig.title: Crossing a narrow channel
lines: You: 11 m yacht under sail, 5 kn
Ship 5 M off, coming down the channel
She can only navigate within it

q: At night you are the give-way vessel for this ship, which sees your green sidelight. You turn to starboard to pass astern of her. How far must you turn before she sees your red light instead?
a: More than 45° — until she is on your port bow
o: More than 22.5° — the edge of your sidelight
10° at a time, so that she sees you turn
More than 90° — until she sees your stern
why: She bears 045° relative: past a 45° turn she is on your port bow and sees your red — a bold, obvious alteration (Rules 8, 16).

fig.note: Night · she bears 045° relative · steady

q: Motoring up this narrow channel at night, you are catching up a ship that can only navigate within it. She must move over for you to pass on her port side. What do you sound?
a: Two prolonged, two short — then wait for her reply
o: Two prolonged, one short — then wait for her reply
Two prolonged, two short — then pass at once
Two short blasts — you are altering to port
why: Rule 34(c): 2 prolonged + 2 short = I intend to overtake on your port side; go only after her prolonged-short-prolonged-short.

fig.note: Night · narrow channel · you are gaining on her

q: Arriving tired at 0300, your crew suggests anchoring at the edge of this channel, just outside the harbour, until daylight. What does Rule 9 say?
a: Avoid anchoring in a narrow channel
o: Fine — at the starboard edge, out of the way
Fine — as long as your anchor light is on
Fine — boats under 20 m can't impede ships
why: Rule 9(g): every vessel shall, if the circumstances of the case admit, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel.

fig.note: Narrow buoyed channel · 0300

q: Motoring west along the westbound lane of a scheme at night, you see these lights dead ahead — a vessel coming the wrong way up your lane. What do you do?
a: Alter to starboard — Rule 14 still applies
o: Hold on — she is in the wrong lane, she gives way
Alter to port — keep her on your starboard side
Stop in the lane and sound five short blasts
why: Rule 10(a): a scheme does not lift any other rule — head-on, both alter to starboard (Rule 14).

fig.note: Night · dead ahead in your lane · steady

q: You cross this scheme to the north at night, on the heading Rule 10 asks for. How long are you in it, and where do you come out?
a: 70 min — 2.3 M east of straight across
o: 74 min — straight across, no set
70 min — straight across, no set
70 min — 2.3 M west of straight across
why: Heading 000°T at 6 kn: 7.0 M ÷ 6 kn = 70 min; the stream sets you 2.0 kn × 70/60 h = 2.3 M east.

fig.note: Traffic separation scheme · north up

q: Running dead downwind with your mainsail out to starboard, you converge with this yacht beating to windward. Who keeps clear?
a: You — main to starboard means port tack
o: She does — you are on starboard tack
She does — a running yacht has right of way
She does — she is the windward yacht
why: Rule 12(b): the windward side is the side opposite the mainsail — main to starboard means port tack, so you keep clear.

fig.note: Mainsail out to starboard · converging

q: Under sail on a dark night, you are slowly closing this light. Its bearing hardly changes. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you are overtaking her, even under sail
o: She does — power gives way to sail
She does — she is on your starboard bow
Neither — she is at anchor, pass her close
why: Rule 13: seeing only her sternlight, you come up from over 22.5° abaft her beam — the overtaking vessel keeps clear.

fig.note: Night · starboard bow · closing far slower than 6 kn

q: Motoring up on this yacht's starboard quarter, you see her sternlight, then her green as she yaws, then the sternlight again. Who keeps clear?
a: You — in doubt, you are the overtaking vessel
o: She does — her green shows you are crossing
She does — you are on her starboard side
Neither — hold on and sound five short
why: Rule 13(c): when in any doubt whether you are overtaking, assume that you are, and keep out of her way.

fig.note: Night · on your port bow · she is yawing

q: A minute ago this ship, dead ahead, was showing you both sidelights. Now you see this. What is she doing?
a: Turning to starboard — expect a port-to-port pass
o: Turning to port — expect a starboard-to-starboard pass
Holding her course — her red says she stands on
Going astern — her masthead lights have closed up
why: Her lower, forward masthead light has opened to your left and only her red shows: her bow is swinging to her starboard.

fig.note: Night · dead ahead, 1.5 M

q: You are the stand-on vessel under power. She did not answer your five short blasts and is now 2 cables off on your port beam, showing these lights. What do you do?
a: Turn hard to starboard, away from her, now
o: Hold on — keeping clear is still her job
Stop your engine and let her pass ahead
Turn hard to port, to cross ahead of her
why: Rule 17(b): she alone can no longer avoid you, so you must act — turn away from her, never to port towards her (17(c)).

fig.note: Night · port beam, 2 cables · both sidelights

q: You were the stand-on vessel; she did not give way, so you turned to avoid her. What does Rule 17 say about your crew's remark?
a: Wrong — she still has to keep out of your way
o: Right — whoever acts first takes on the duty
Right — once you have turned, Rule 17 ends
Wrong — now you both must stop your engines
why: Rule 17(d): action by the stand-on vessel does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way.

fig.title: After your alteration
lines: You stood on; she did not give way
You turned to starboard to avoid her

q: Beating to windward with the mainsail up and the engine running to help, you converge with this yacht under sail alone. Who keeps clear?
a: You — with the engine on you are power-driven
o: She does — she's on port tack, you're on starboard
She does — you are on her starboard side
Both alter to starboard, as if head-on
why: Rule 3(b): a sailing vessel with her engine in use is power-driven — Rule 18(a): you keep out of the way of a vessel under sail.

fig.note: Mainsail up, engine in gear · bearing steady

q: Under sail off Ithaca, you come up on this coaster lying stopped across your course with this shape hoisted. Who keeps clear?
a: You — she is not under command
o: She does — power gives way to sail
She does — she is only at anchor
You — she is aground on a shoal
why: Rules 27(a) and 18(b): two balls in a vertical line mean not under command; a sailing vessel keeps out of her way.

fig.note: Day · stopped across your course

q: Sailing across the approach to Thessaloniki, you see this tanker coming up the dredged channel with this shape. What does Rule 18 ask of you?
a: Avoid impeding her — she is constrained by draught
o: Nothing — a power vessel gives way to sail
Keep clear only if she is on your starboard side
Nothing until she sounds five short blasts
why: Rules 28 and 18(d): a cylinder means constrained by her draught — every vessel but NUC or RAM avoids impeding her.

fig.note: Day · a tanker in the dredged channel

q: Under engine off Lefkada, you come up on this small boat with this shape hoisted. What is she telling you?
a: She is engaged in fishing — keep clear
o: She is motor-sailing — she keeps clear
She is aground — keep off the shoal
She is at anchor — pass either side
why: Rule 26: two cones, points together, mean a vessel engaged in fishing; Rule 18(a): power keeps out of her way.

fig.note: Day · lying stopped

q: Motoring in fog, you have been watching this ship on radar. Now she comes out of the murk, as the card shows. Which rules govern what you do now?
a: The crossing rules — you are now in sight
o: Rule 19 — the fog has not lifted yet
Rule 19 — she was a radar contact first
None — in fog each vessel acts for herself
why: Rule 19 is for vessels not in sight; once in sight, Rules 11–18 apply — she is on your starboard side, so you give way.

fig.title: Fog, under power
lines: A radar contact for ten minutes
She comes into sight 4 cables off
On your starboard bow, crossing to port

q: In fog you plot this radar target twice. What is the CPA, and what do you do?
a: CPA about 0.3 M — alter boldly to starboard
o: CPA about 0.3 M — alter boldly to port
CPA about 1.5 M — no risk, hold on
CPA about 0.3 M — hold on, you stand on
why: Plot: closing 7.5 kn, CPA 0.3 M at about 0348 — close quarters; Rule 19(d): she is forward of the beam, so no turn to port.

q: In fog this radar target is coming up on your starboard quarter, CPA 1 cable. You decide to alter course. Which way?
a: To port, turning away from her side
o: To starboard — always starboard in fog
Neither — she is overtaking, she keeps clear
To starboard, to cross ahead of her
why: Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid an alteration of course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam — here, no turn to starboard.

fig.note: Fog · radar only · closing from astern

q: Motoring at night, you are catching up this tug with a barge lashed alongside her. What lights do you see from astern?
a: Two white sternlights side by side, no yellow
o: A yellow towing light above a white sternlight
Two masthead lights in a vertical line
One white sternlight, a yellow one beside it
why: Rule 24(c),(f): towing alongside, the tug shows a sternlight but no towing light; the barge alongside shows her own sternlight.

fig.note: Night · you are gaining from astern

q: On a clear night you are motoring towards this ship, head-on. Her masthead light first shows at the range Rule 22 gives it. If neither of you alters, how long before you meet?
a: About 15 minutes
o: About 20 minutes
About 30 minutes
About 12 minutes
why: Over 50 m, her masthead light carries 6 M; closing at 18 + 6 = 24 kn, 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 h = 15 min.

fig.title: Head-on, clear night
lines: Her lights seen at their rule ranges

q: Radar puts this ship 5 M off on your starboard bow. You see only these two white lights. Which way is she heading, and why no sidelights?
a: To your right — sidelights carry only 3 M
o: To your left — sidelights carry only 3 M
To your right — her sidelights are off
To your left — her sidelights are off
why: Her lower, forward masthead light is right of the higher aft one; a ship's masthead light carries 6 M, her sidelights 3 M.

fig.note: Night · starboard bow, 5 M on radar

q: After dinner ashore you take this tender back out to the boat. What light does Rule 23 ask her to show?
a: An all-round white; sidelights if practicable
o: None — tenders under 7 m are exempt from lights
Sidelights and a sternlight, like a yacht
A torch, shown only if a ship comes near
why: Rule 23(d)(ii): a power-driven vessel under 7 m, top speed 7 kn or less, may show an all-round white light instead.

q: These lights cross ahead of you from right to left, the two reds well apart. What is she?
a: A tug pushing a barge ahead of her
o: A tug towing a barge astern of her
A ship over 50 m, crossing to your left
Two power vessels, one overtaking the other
why: Rule 24(c),(f): pushing ahead, the tug shows two masthead lights in a line; the barge shows sidelights at her forward end.

fig.note: Night · crossing ahead, right to left

q: Motoring at night, you see these lights crossing ahead of you from left to right. What lies between the two green lights?
a: A towline — never pass between them
o: Open water — they are two separate vessels
A barge pushed ahead of the tug
A fishing net strung between two boats
why: Rule 24: two masthead lights in a line mean towing; the tow's own green, astern of the tug, marks the end of the towline.

fig.note: Night · crossing ahead, left to right

q: Under sail by day, you are about to cross the track of this tug and her tow. What do the shapes tell you?
a: A tow over 200 m — pass astern of the barge
o: A short tow — you may cross between them
She is aground — keep clear of both
She is restricted — pass on either side
why: Rule 24(a)(v),(e)(iii): a diamond on the tug and another on the tow mean a tow longer than 200 m.

fig.title: By day, ahead
lines: A tug with a black diamond shape
A barge far astern of her, 400 m

q: You take this disabled yacht in tow for the night run to harbour. Your boat has no towing lights. What do you show?
a: Your usual lights, and a light on the towline
o: Two all-round reds — you can't manoeuvre
Your anchor light too — you are barely moving
The tricolour — you are as slow as a sailboat
why: Rule 24(i): a vessel not normally towing needn't show towing lights, but must show the tow — in particular by lighting the towline.

q: Under sail at night, you see these two tugs, each with a tow, crossing ahead on steady bearings. Who keeps clear of whom?
a: A keeps clear of you; you keep clear of B
o: You keep clear of both — tugs have priority
Both keep clear of you — power gives way to sail
You keep clear of A; B keeps clear of you
why: Rule 18: towing alone gives no priority; Rule 27(c): red-white-red means B can't deviate, so you keep out of her way.

q: Your new yacht has all these lights on her switch panel. Under sail alone at night, which combination may you show?
a: Red-over-green with the bow and stern lights
o: Red-over-green together with the tricolour
The tricolour together with the steaming light
Red-over-green on its own, nothing else
why: Rule 25(c): red-over-green may be added to the sidelights and sternlight, but is never shown with the tricolour.

fig.title: Switch panel, 14 m yacht
lines: Bow and stern lights · Steaming light

q: Motoring at night, you see these lights dead ahead, closing. What is she?
a: A yacht motoring with her tricolour on
o: A yacht under sail, correctly lit
A power boat under 12 m, correctly lit
A yacht under sail, showing red-over-green
why: Rule 25(b): the tricolour is for sailing only; a white light on the mast below it is a steaming light — treat her as power.

fig.note: Night · dead ahead, closing · nothing lower

q: Under sail at night, you see only these two lights on your starboard bow, the bearing drawing slowly aft. What is she doing?
a: Trawling, but stopped — not making way
o: Trawling and making way, end-on to you
Piloting, stopped on her station
Lying at anchor, 50 m or more long
why: Rule 26(b): green over white means trawling; the sidelights and sternlight are shown only when making way through the water.

fig.note: Night · starboard bow · nothing else visible

q: Motoring at night, you are slowly catching up these lights. What is she, and what do you do?
a: A trawler seen from astern — keep well clear
o: A trawler seen from ahead — hold your course
A pilot boat seen from astern — keep well clear
A trawler at anchor — pass her either side
why: Rule 26(b): green over white, a sternlight below — a trawler making way, you astern; Rule 13: the overtaking vessel keeps clear.

fig.note: Night · ahead · you are slowly gaining

q: Your crew wants to call MAYDAY RELAY for this ship, which shows only these lights. What do you tell them?
a: No — she is not under command, not in distress
o: Yes — two reds mean a ship in distress
No — she is aground and in no danger
Yes — a ship with no way on needs rescue
why: Rule 27(a),(h): two all-round reds mean not under command, and are not distress signals; no sidelights, so no way on.

fig.note: Night · 1 M off · no sidelights, not moving

q: Motoring at night, you have this vessel ahead, working and not moving. On which side do you pass her?
a: On the side of the two greens, to your right
o: On the side of the two reds, to your left
Either side — she is only at anchor
Neither — keep 1000 m off her all round
why: Rule 27(d): red-white-red is RAM; two reds mark the side of the obstruction, two greens the side where you may pass.

fig.note: Night · ahead · working, not moving

q: Motoring at night, you see these lights about 2 M ahead. How close may you pass her?
a: No closer than 1000 m
o: No closer than 500 m
As close as you like, on her green side
Within 200 m, but only astern of her
why: Rule 27(f): three all-round greens mean mine clearance — it is dangerous to come within 1000 m of her.

fig.note: Night · about 2 M ahead

q: Arriving off the entrance at night, you see these lights. They don't move, and as you pass round her no sidelight ever shows. What is she?
a: A pilot vessel on duty, at anchor
o: A pilot vessel on duty, under way
A vessel fishing, at anchor
A vessel aground, under 50 m
why: Rule 29: white over red is a pilot vessel on duty; at anchor she adds her anchor light and shows no sidelights.

fig.note: Night · off the entrance · not moving

q: Coming into the anchorage off Piraeus at night, you see these lights on a ship that is not moving. What is she?
a: A ship at anchor, 50 m or more long
o: A ship under way, seen from ahead
A ship aground, waiting for the tide
A ship towing, seen from astern
why: Rule 30(a),(c): two all-round whites, the forward one higher than the after one; a big ship also lights her decks.

fig.note: Night · not moving · decks lit

q: You anchor your 13 m yacht overnight in a bay off Paxos. Which switch on this panel do you put on?
a: Anchor — the all-round white light
o: Tricolour — it is seen all round
Nav — bow and stern, so you are seen
Steaming — a white light forward is enough
why: Rule 30(b): a vessel under 50 m at anchor may show one all-round white light where it can best be seen.

q: At 0200 you took this single white light ahead for a sternlight. You have since passed round her and have her abeam, 2 cables off, and it is still all you see. What is she?
a: A yacht at anchor — the light is all-round
o: A yacht under way — it is her sternlight
A yacht under sail — it is her tricolour
A yacht under power — it is her steaming light
why: Rule 21: from abeam an under-way yacht shows a sidelight; one white seen from every side is an anchor light (Rule 30(b)).

fig.note: Night · abeam, 2 cables · a yacht of about 12 m

q: Leaving harbour at night, you watch this ferry ahead of you at her berth. What is she telling you?
a: I am operating astern propulsion
o: I am altering my course to starboard
I am altering my course to port
I am in doubt about your intentions
why: Rule 34(a),(b): three short blasts, or three flashes of the all-round white light, mean I am operating astern propulsion.

fig.title: Night, at the ferry quay
lines: Ferry ahead, lines just let go

q: In fog off the Brittany coast, you are under main and engine. Your crew reaches for the horn to sound the sailing-vessel signal. What should you sound?
a: One prolonged blast every two minutes or less
o: One prolonged and two short every two minutes
Two prolonged blasts every two minutes or less
One short, one prolonged and one short
why: With the engine in use you are power-driven (Rule 3(b)); making way, Rule 35(a): one prolonged blast at most 2 min apart.

q: In fog you hear the signal in the card, repeated, from the same spot for twenty minutes. Which of these could she be?
a: A vessel engaged in fishing, at anchor
o: A power vessel stopped and drifting
A vessel aground on the bank
A ship over 100 m, at anchor
why: Rule 35(d): a vessel fishing at anchor, or RAM at work at anchor, sounds 1 prolonged + 2 short instead of the bell.

fig.title: Fog, listening
lines: One prolonged and two short blasts

q: Groping towards the harbour in fog, you hear the signal in the card ahead of you, repeated each minute. What does it tell you?
a: A vessel aground — the shoal is close
o: A vessel at anchor, over 100 m long
A vessel at anchor, under 20 m long
A vessel engaged in fishing, at anchor
why: Rule 35(h): three separate and distinct strokes on the bell before and after the rapid ringing mean a vessel aground.

fig.title: Fog, near a shoal
lines: Three separate strokes on a bell

q: Motoring in fog in your 11 m yacht, your crew says boats this small need no fog signal at all. What does Rule 35 say?
a: Some efficient sound signal every 2 minutes
o: Nothing — boats under 12 m are exempt
Only a bell, rung rapidly every minute
Only once you hear another vessel's signal
why: Rule 35(j): under 12 m you needn't give the full signals, but then you must make some other efficient sound signal at most 2 min apart.

fig.title: Fog, visibility 1 cable
lines: Your 11 m yacht, motoring at 4 kn

q: In fog off the port entrance, you hear the signal in the card, repeated. What is she?
a: A pilot vessel on duty, making way
o: A vessel aground, warning you off
A tug followed by her manned tow
A vessel in doubt about your intentions
why: Rule 35(k): a pilot vessel on duty may add four short blasts, her identity signal, to her normal fog signal.

fig.title: Fog, off the entrance
lines: Then at once: four short blasts

q: Dismasted 5 M off the coast, your crew lays out this kit to signal distress. Which of these is not a distress signal?
a: A white handheld flare
o: A red parachute rocket
An orange smoke signal
A red handheld flare
why: Annex IV lists red rockets, red flares and orange smoke; a white flare only draws attention (Rule 36).

q: By day you see these two yachts a mile off. Which of them is signalling distress?
a: A — N over C is a distress signal
o: B — V is the distress flag
Both — any code flag asks for help
Neither — flags are never distress signals
why: Annex IV(f): the code flags N over C mean distress; flag V asks for assistance but is not a distress signal.

fig.title: A mile off, by day
lines: Yacht A flies code flags N over C
Yacht B flies code flag V
Both lying still in a calm
